transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, yeah… thanks for seeing me. I guess the main thing is work has been getting harder in a way that’s kind of embarrassing. I process insurance claims, and I’m supposed to stay at my workstation and get through reviews, but I keep getting up during the day—like, more than I probably should—even when I know I need to just sit there and finish. It’s not that I’m trying to avoid work, exactly… I just keep leaving my seat, and it’s starting to feel like a problem.
When you get up from your workstation, is it because you feel you have to check or repeat something?

Um… I don’t think so. Not like I’m checking the same thing over and over, if that’s what you mean. I mean, I might tell myself I’m getting water or going to look at something, but it doesn’t feel like I have to repeat something exactly. I haven’t really noticed that pattern, anyway.
When you get up from your workstation, do you feel physically restless?

Yeah… I think so, a little. I mean, I wouldn’t say I’m like pacing around or anything, but in trainings or longer team meetings I catch myself bouncing my leg, clicking my pen, shifting around in the chair. I try to look like I’m paying attention and being normal about it, but it’s kind of constant sometimes. Does that count as physically restless?
Have there been times when you felt unusually energetic or wired for days at a time?

Um… I don’t think so? Not like days at a time where I’m wired or unusually energized. I might have a day where I drink too much coffee or I’m stressed and feel kind of keyed up, but I wouldn’t say it goes on for days or feels, like, out of character. Is that what you mean?
When you were a child, did teachers or family often describe you as fidgety or unable to stay seated?

Um… I don’t remember being told I was, like, the kid constantly running around or refusing to sit down. But looking back, it wasn’t exactly brand new either. In elementary school, teachers would write things like I was bright, but I’d lose worksheets, miss instructions, or need reminders to finish my classwork.

So maybe not “fidgety” in a big disruptive way, but there were definitely comments that I had trouble staying on track, if that answers it.
Before you turned 12, were you already having trouble staying focused or finishing tasks?

Yeah, I think so… I mean, I don’t want to make it sound worse than it was, because I did okay in school in some ways. But looking back, it wasn’t really new. In elementary school, teachers would say I was bright, but I’d lose worksheets, miss instructions, and need reminders to finish my classwork. So… yes, I guess that was already happening before 12.
Do you notice the same trouble staying focused or seated in other parts of your life besides work?

Um… I’m not totally sure. I guess outside of work I don’t usually think of it that way, because I’m not being watched or graded, you know? I can sit through things if I need to, mostly.

With focus… maybe sometimes at home, but I don’t know if it’s enough to count. Like I might drift off during chores or while someone’s talking, but I feel like everybody does that sometimes. I’m not sure if that’s the kind of thing you’re asking about.
Do you often feel excessively worried or on edge, even when there isn’t an immediate problem to deal with?

Um… I don’t think so, not excessively. I mean, I worry about normal stuff—work, bills, whether I’m keeping up—but I wouldn’t say I’m constantly on edge when nothing’s happening.

At least, I don’t think that’s a big thing for me. I’m not sure if that’s what you mean.
Do these focus problems happen in more than one setting, like at home or in conversations with other people?

Yeah… I mean, I think so. It’s not like it only started at work or anything. Looking back, even in elementary school, teachers would put things like that I was bright, but I’d lose worksheets or miss instructions, and they’d have to remind me to finish classwork.

So… I guess that does sound like it was showing up in more than one kind of setting, at least school and now other situations. I don’t know if I’m explaining that the right way.

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview supports attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder with childhood onset and persistence into adulthood. Confirmed symptoms include longstanding inattention (losing worksheets, missing instructions, needing reminders to finish tasks, drifting off) and some hyperactive/restless features (leaving workstation, leg bouncing, pen clicking, shifting in seat). Onset before age 12 was explicitly confirmed, and symptoms are present across settings (childhood school and current work/other situations). Anxiety, mania, and compulsive checking were not supported as primary explanations.
